accepted_findings.summary: The reported administrator interview sample is internally inconsistent (14 in the abstract versus 12 in methods), leaving the qualitative evidentiary base unclear.
The analysis excludes dissenting cases for not fitting the three-theme structure while claiming balanced, full-range representation; this selectively constructs the thematic account.
The discussion reverses Delacroix's stated position on stakeholder consultation, so a central design recommendation rests on a contradictory attribution.
The discussion makes sector-wide and universal claims from a three-university, single-national-system study without evidentiary support for that transfer.
Claimed full anonymization is inconsistent with role-and-institution descriptions that may enable deductive identification in the small sample.
The thematic-analysis description lacks the procedural and cross-case evidence needed to assess coding dependability, saturation, and the assertion that themes are not institution-specific.
The staff survey is treated as corroboration of administrator experiences despite sampling a different role group and reporting insufficient integration detail.
Recruitment through institutional QA offices presents unaddressed gatekeeping and social-desirability risks.
The manuscript's claim to be the first comprehensive administrator account is overstated relative to its own cited administrator- and quality-office-focused literature.

synthesis.rationale: Multiple P1 defects affect the qualitative evidentiary base, representation of participant views, citation accuracy, claim calibration, and participant confidentiality.
